intro-statistics-s1.title: A study room at lunch
intro-statistics-s1.html: A high school has 2,400 students. The student council wants to know whether students would use a quiet study room at lunch. The council chooses 120 students at random from the school list and asks each one, "Would you use a quiet study room at lunch once a week or more?" Of the 120 students, 78 answer yes (invented data).

intro-statistics-s2.html: A health teacher wants to learn how many hours of sleep students in her district get on school nights. The district has 6 high schools with 9,000 students in all. She asks 60 students from her own school, each in one of her classes, to record their sleep for one week (invented data).

investigative-questions-s1.title: Walking and blood pressure
investigative-questions-s1.html: A health researcher studied the medical records of 1,200 adults in a city. Adults whose records said they walked 30 minutes or more a day had a lower typical blood pressure than adults who walked less. The researcher did not ask anyone to change how much they walk (invented data).

investigative-questions-s2.title: Phones at lunch
investigative-questions-s2.html:
The student council at Lincoln High School, which has 1,500 students, wants to learn about phone use during lunch. Members suggest four questions:

  1. Do you like your phone?
  2. What proportion of Lincoln High students use a phone during lunch on a typical school day?
  3. Do phones cause students to eat less at lunch?
  4. How many minutes did Maria spend on her phone at lunch today?

random-sampling-s1.title: Four ways to sample a school
random-sampling-s1.html:
A high school has 1,200 students: 300 in each of grades 9, 10, 11 and 12, in 48 homerooms of 25 students. The principal wants about 100 students’ opinions on a new schedule. Four plans:

  • Plan P: number the students from 1 to 1,200 and use a random number generator to choose 100 different numbers.
  • Plan Q: choose 25 students at random from each grade.
  • Plan R: choose 4 of the 48 homerooms at random and survey every student in them.
  • Plan S: list the students alphabetically, choose a random starting point among the first 12, then take every 12th student.

random-sampling-s2.title: Testing pond water
random-sampling-s2.html: A park has 80 ponds, listed on a park map. A wildlife team has the time and equipment to test the water in 10 of them, and wants a simple random sample of 10 ponds.

sampling-problems-s1.title: A survey about a parking fee
sampling-problems-s1.html:
A city council wants to know what proportion of the city’s adult residents oppose a new fee for parking downtown. Three plans are proposed:

  • Plan 1: post a link on the city website inviting residents to answer one question.
  • Plan 2: interview shoppers on the main downtown street on a weekday afternoon.
  • Plan 3: mail a survey to 500 adults chosen at random from the list of registered voters. Only 210 mail it back.

sampling-problems-s2.title: Two ways to ask
sampling-problems-s2.html:
Two versions of a survey question were written about the same fee.

  • Version A: "Do you support a small fee to keep downtown streets clean and safe?"
  • Version B: "Do you support a new tax on drivers who visit downtown?"

experimental-design-s1.title: Blue-light glasses and sleep
experimental-design-s1.html: A researcher recruits 60 college students who volunteer for a sleep study. A random number generator assigns 30 of them to wear glasses that block blue light for two hours before bed, and the other 30 to wear clear glasses that look exactly the same. After two weeks, each student’s sleep quality is scored from a sleep tracker. Neither the students nor the person scoring the trackers knows who wore which glasses (invented study).

experimental-design-s2.title: Two training programs
experimental-design-s2.html: A gym wants to compare two six-week training programs, P and Q, for increasing the number of push-ups members can do. Forty members volunteer: 16 are beginners and 24 are experienced. The plan: within the beginners, assign 8 to P and 8 to Q at random; within the experienced members, assign 12 to P and 12 to Q at random. Each member’s gain in push-ups is recorded (invented study).

items.q: What is the mean battery life, in hours?

mistakes.why: That is the median. The mean adds all 12 values and divides by 12.
That divides the sum by 11. There are 12 phones, so divide by 12.

items.q: What is the median battery life, in hours?

mistakes.why: That is the 7th value alone. With 12 values the median is the average of the 6th and 7th: (9.3 + 9.5)/2.
That is the mean. The median is the middle of the ordered values.

items.q: What is the interquartile range (IQR) of the battery lives, in hours?

mistakes.why: That is the range, maximum minus minimum. The IQR is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3 - Q_1</annotation></semantics></math>.

That subtracts the two middle values of the whole data set, 9.5 − 9.3. <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3</annotation></semantics></math> are the medians of the lower and upper halves.

items.q: What is the standard deviation of the battery lives, in hours? Use the sample standard deviation.

mistakes.why: That divides by <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 12</annotation></semantics></math>. The sample standard deviation divides by <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1 = 11</annotation></semantics></math>.
That is the variance, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^2</annotation></semantics></math>. Take its square root.

items.q: Which battery lives are outliers by the <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo>×</mo><mtext>IQR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5 \times \text{IQR}</annotation></semantics></math> rule?

options: No: the upper fence is 460 + 1.5(460) = 1,150
No: the upper fence is 460 + 1.5(980 − 210) = 1,615
Yes, because the maximum of a data set is an outlier by definition

The sample standard deviation divides by <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1 = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>

mistakes.why: That is the 5th value. The lower half has 10 values, so <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_1</annotation></semantics></math> is the average of its 5th and 6th values: (13 + 14)/2.

items.q: What is the upper fence, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo>×</mo><mtext>IQR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}</annotation></semantics></math>, in minutes?

mistakes.why: That adds just one IQR to <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3</annotation></semantics></math>. The fence adds <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo>×</mo><mtext>IQR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5 \times \text{IQR}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>13.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1.5(13.5)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>20.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 20.25</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: A sample survey asks 400 adults whether they recycle. What kind of study is a sample survey?
options: An observational study that asks questions
An experiment, since the adults have to answer the questions
A census
A study that can show recycling causes changes in behavior

items.q: What kind of sample does plan P give?
options: A stratified random sample
A simple random sample
A cluster sample
A systematic random sample, since a generator is used

items.q: What kind of sample does plan Q give?
options: A cluster sample, with the grades as the clusters
A simple random sample of 100 of the school’s students
A systematic random sample of 25 students per grade
A stratified random sample, with the grades as strata

items.q: What kind of sample does plan R give, and what is its main advantage?
options: A cluster sample: whole homerooms make it easy
A stratified sample: it guarantees that each grade is included
A simple random sample: each student has the same chance of selection
A systematic sample

items.q: The principal thinks opinions on the schedule differ a lot from grade to grade. Which plan best makes sure each grade’s view is represented?
options: Plan R
Plan P
Plan Q
Plan S

items.q: In plan S, about how many students end up in the sample?
Put the steps for choosing the simple random sample of 10 ponds in order.
options: Label the 80 ponds on the map with the numbers 1 to 80
Use a random number generator to produce whole numbers from 1 to 80
Skip any number that has already been chosen
Keep going until 10 different numbers are chosen
Test the water in the 10 ponds with those numbers

items.q: A team member writes, "Use a random number generator to pick 10 ponds." Why is this not enough as a procedure?
options: It leaves out labeling 1 to 80 and handling repeats
A random number generator gives the same pond each time
Ten ponds is too few
Ponds have to be picked from a table, not from a generator

items.q: Why skip a number that has already been chosen?
options: To sample with replacement, so a pond can be tested twice
Because a random number generator does not repeat numbers it has given
To enlarge the sample
To sample without replacement

items.q: What is the sampling frame in this study?
options: The 10 ponds tested
The park map listing the 80 ponds
The water quality in each pond that is tested
The equipment that the team uses for testing water

items.q: What makes a sample a simple random sample of size n?
options: Each group of n has the same chance of being chosen
The people chosen are the first n to arrive at a location
Each subgroup of the population appears in the sample
The researcher picks n individuals who seem typical

items.q: How should strata differ from clusters?
options: Strata are chosen at random, and clusters are chosen by the researcher
Strata are larger groups of people than clusters
Strata hold similar individuals; clusters each mix the population
Strata and clusters are two names for the same idea

items.q: A city takes every 10th house along each street, starting at a random house among the first 10. On every street, every 10th house is a corner house, which tends to be larger. What is the problem?
options: Systematic samples are too small to say anything about a city
The list repeats with the same step of 10
The starting house was chosen at random, which is not allowed
Corner houses are unusual

items.q: Names are drawn from a hat for a 3-person committee, and each name is put back after it is drawn. What is the problem?
options: Drawing names from a hat is not random enough for a committee
Putting names back makes each person less likely to be chosen
Three is too few
It allows one person to be drawn twice

items.q: Which of these are random sampling methods? Select all that apply.
options: Choosing 50 names with a random number generator from a numbered list
Choosing 10 people at random from each of 5 neighborhoods
Asking the first 50 people who walk into a store
Choosing the 50 people whom the interviewer thinks look friendly

items.q: A city’s neighborhoods differ a lot in income, and a planner wants to estimate typical household spending on transport. Which design fits best?
options: Take the households on the busiest street in the city
Stratify by neighborhood
Choose one neighborhood at random and survey each of its homes
Ask the planner’s friends

items.q: What is a sampling frame?
options: The sample size
The question that the survey asks each individual
The time period during which the data are collected
The list a sample is drawn from

items.q: What kind of sample does plan 1 produce?
options: A convenience sample
A voluntary response sample
A simple random sample
A cluster sample of website visitors

items.q: How is plan 1 likely to be biased?
options: It likely underestimates the proportion who oppose the fee
It has no bias, since each resident can reach the website
It gives the exact proportion, because many people respond
It likely overestimates the proportion who oppose the fee

items.q: Which problem does plan 2 have?
options: A convenience sample of people downtown
It is a voluntary response sample of downtown shoppers
It has undercoverage of shoppers who drive downtown
Response bias by mail

items.q: Only 210 of the 500 adults in plan 3 mailed the survey back. What is this problem called?
options: Undercoverage
Voluntary response
Nonresponse
Response bias

items.q: Plan 3 draws its sample from the list of registered voters. Which problem does that frame create?
options: Nonresponse: registered voters are less likely to answer mailed surveys
Voluntary response: registered voters choose to be on the list
Undercoverage of residents who are not registered
No problem

items.q: What kind of problem can wording like this cause?
options: Response bias
Undercoverage
Nonresponse
Convenience sampling

items.q: Which version is likely to get more "yes" answers, and why?
options: Version B: "new tax" makes the idea sound more official to people
Version B: naming drivers makes it clearer who would pay
Neither version
Version A: its words make the fee sound appealing

items.q: Which wording is the most neutral?
options: "Do you agree that a fee would keep downtown clean?"
"Do you support or oppose a 2-dollar parking fee?"
"Should drivers be forced to pay yet another fee?"
"Most residents support the fee. Do you?"

items.q: The council asks Version A of 2,000 adults chosen at random instead of 500. What happens to the response bias?
options: It stays: a larger sample repeats the same push in the wording
It shrinks to nothing, because the sample is four times larger
It shrinks a little, because random sampling cancels wording effects
It reverses, because a big sample includes more people who disagree

items.q: What does it mean for a sampling method to be biased?
options: Its results vary a little from one sample to the next
The researcher has opinions
It errs in the same direction again and again
It uses a sample that is smaller than the population

items.q: A talk show asks viewers to text in their opinion of a new law; 50,000 viewers respond and 85% oppose the law. What is the best criticism?
options: 50,000 responses is too small for a law that affects millions
Viewers chose to respond, so strong views are overrepresented
Texting costs money, so the results are illegal to report
85% is too high a result to be a real survey finding

items.q: A survey phones only landline numbers. Which group is most likely undercovered?
options: Older adults who answer their landline
People who live in houses with phones
Residents who refuse to answer the survey
Young adults who have only mobile phones

items.q: A teacher asks students face to face, "Have you ever cheated on a test?" What is the most likely effect?
options: Nonresponse from absences
Response bias: some may deny cheating
Undercoverage: students who cheat are not on the class list
Voluntary response: students choose to answer the question

items.q: A student explains why a convenience sample is a problem: "The sample is too small." Which explanation would earn credit instead?
options: The researcher may have made arithmetic errors in the results
A convenience sample takes too long to collect
The sample is too small to calculate a percent
Easy-to-reach people may differ from the population

items.q: Which of these is an example of nonresponse? Select all that apply.
options: Of 800 randomly chosen households, 300 never answer the door
A survey frame leaves out people living in dormitories
A question asks, "Don’t you agree that taxes are too high?"
A website invites anyone to fill in a form about a new park

items.q: A random sample of 600 adults is chosen from a complete list of a city’s adults. Which problem can still occur?
options: Nonresponse or response bias
Voluntary response bias in the sample
Convenience sampling by the interviewers
Undercoverage

items.q: What are the experimental units?
options: The glasses
The 60 students
The sleep quality scores
The sleep trackers worn by the students

items.q: What are the treatments, and what is the response variable?
options: Treatments: the 60 students. Response: the type of glasses worn
Treatments: sleep quality scores. Response: the two kinds of glasses
Treatments: the sleep trackers. Response: the time spent in bed
Treatments: the two kinds of glasses. Response: sleep quality

items.q: Why do half the students wear clear glasses that look the same?
options: To act as a placebo, so both groups believe they may be treated
To make the study cheaper, since clear glasses cost less
To make sure that each student sleeps for the same number of hours
To let the students choose the glasses that they like better

items.q: Neither the students nor the person scoring the trackers knows who wore which glasses. What is this called?
options: A single-blind experiment
A matched pairs experiment
A double-blind experiment
An observational study of sleep

items.q: What does random assignment allow the researcher to conclude?
options: The results apply to college students across the country
Each student’s own sleep will improve with blue-light glasses
A large difference was likely caused by the glasses
The two groups were exactly alike before the study began

items.q: What is this design called?
options: A randomized block design
A completely randomized design
A matched pairs design
A stratified random sample

items.q: Why does the gym block by experience?
options: So that beginners get program P and experienced members get program Q
To make sure the gym has the same number of beginners and experienced members
Because experienced members would refuse to train with beginners
Experience affects gains, so comparing within blocks removes that variation

items.q: Put the steps for assigning the 16 beginners to the programs in order.
options: Write the 16 beginners’ names on identical slips of paper
Mix the slips well in a container
Draw 8 slips without looking
Assign those 8 beginners to program P
Assign the other 8 beginners to program Q

items.q: Members in program P gain many more push-ups than members in Q, too many to be explained by chance in the assignment. What can the gym conclude?
options: P causes larger gains for gym members across the country
P causes larger gains for members like these volunteers
P is linked to larger gains, but no cause can be claimed
Nothing can be concluded, as the blocks have different sizes

items.q: To test two sunscreens, each of 20 volunteers gets sunscreen A on one arm and B on the other, with a coin flip deciding which arm gets A. What design is this?
options: A matched pairs design
One sunscreen per volunteer
An observational study
A cluster sample of arms

items.q: In experimental design, what does replication mean?
options: Copying another researcher’s experiment exactly
Measuring each unit twice to check the measurement
Giving each treatment to enough experimental units
Using one treatment on each unit

items.q: A report says the difference between two treatment groups was statistically significant. What does that mean?
options: The difference is large enough to matter in daily life
The difference is too large to be explained by chance alone
The study proved that the treatment works for everyone
The difference was measured very precisely

items.q: Which is a completely randomized design for comparing two fertilizers on 30 plants?
options: Give fertilizer A to the 15 tallest plants and B to the rest
Let the gardener pick which plants get each fertilizer
Split by sunlight first
Assign 15 plants at random to each fertilizer

items.q: Why do many experiments include a control group?
options: To make sure that each subject receives the new treatment
To give a baseline that the treatment group can be compared with
To reduce the number of subjects that the study needs
To stop subjects from knowing they are in a study

items.q: A teacher lets students choose between a new online study tool and the usual worksheets, then compares test scores. Why is this a weak experiment?
options: The online tool and the worksheets cost different amounts
Test scores are a quantitative response variable
The class has too many students to compare
Self-chosen groups may differ in motivation

items.q: Patients given a sugar pill report less pain, though the pill has no active ingredient. What is this called?
options: The placebo effect
Response bias
Replication of the pain medicine
A confounding variable in the medicine

items.q: Which feature of a study allows a cause-and-effect conclusion? Select all that apply.
options: Random assignment of treatments to units
Random selection of units from a population
Using a large number of volunteers
Measuring many variables on each unit

items.q: In the blue-light study, 60 volunteers were randomly assigned to the two kinds of glasses, and the blue-light group had statistically significantly better sleep quality. Build the scope-of-inference statement.

cause.label: Cause and effect
options: Blue-light glasses cause better sleep quality, because the glasses were randomly assigned
Blue-light glasses are linked to better sleep, but no cause can be claimed
Blue-light glasses cause better sleep, because 60 students is a large sample

why.1: Random assignment of treatments is exactly what allows a cause-and-effect conclusion.
why.2: Sample size does not create a causal conclusion; random assignment does.

scope.label: To whom
options: for students like these volunteers
for all college students
for every person who wears glasses

why.1: The students were volunteers, not a random sample of all college students.
why.2: The study included only college student volunteers.

conclude.model: Because the glasses were randomly assigned and the difference was statistically significant, the study gives evidence that blue-light glasses cause better sleep quality for students like these volunteers; because the students were volunteers and not a random sample, the result should not be generalized to all college students.
